description.text: Livia Drusilla (30 January 59 BC – AD 29) was the Roman empress from 27 BC to AD 14, the wife of Augustus, the first Roman emperor.  She was known as Julia Augusta after her formal adoption into the Julia gens in AD 14.  Livia served as an influential confidante to her husband and was rumoured to have been responsible for the deaths of several of his relatives, including his grandson Agrippa Postumus.

After Augustus died in AD 14, Livia continued to exert political influence as the mother of the emperor until her death in AD 29.  She was deified by Claudius in AD 42, bestowing her the title Diva Augusta, and her legacy was honoured in public games and statues.  Livia’s life and reputation have been the subject of both ancient and modern historical debate, with sources ranging from Tacitus and Cassius Dio to contemporary scholarship.

curiosities.text: Livia owned and effectively administered copper mines in Gaul, estates of palm groves in Judea, and dozens of papyrus marshes in Egypt, and she had her own circle of clients and protégés who were pushed into political offices.
The fig variety Liviana was named after her, possibly as a tongue‑in‑cheek reference to the rumor that she poisoned Augustus’ figs by smearing them with poison while they were still on the tree.
She was the third woman to appear on provincial coins in 16 BC, after Octavia the Younger and Cleopatra, marking her prominence in Roman imperial iconography.
